title: Chapter XXXVIII

teacherSummary.text: On Elizabeth's last morning Collins gives a farewell speech praising his own humble home and his privileged connection with Rosings. Elizabeth pities Charlotte but sees she is content. Elizabeth and Maria travel to London to meet Jane.

vocabulary.definition: A portion of anything taken separately
vocabulary.context: At length the chaise arrived, the trunks were fastened on, the parcels placed within, and it was pronounced to be ready.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “parcel”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Domestic fowls reared for the table, or for their eggs or feathers, such as cocks and hens, capons, turkeys, ducks,…
vocabulary.context: Her home and her housekeeping, her parish and her poultry, and all their dependent concerns, had not yet lost their charms.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “poultry”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Amazement or horror that confounds the faculties, and incapacitates for refletion
vocabulary.context: He then handed her in, Maria followed, and the door was on the point of being closed, when he suddenly reminded them, with some consternation, that they had hitherto forgotten to leave any message for the ladies of Rosings.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “consternation”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of raising from a lower place, condition, or quality to a higher
vocabulary.context: Words were insufficient for the elevation of his feelings; and he was obliged to walk about the room, while Elizabeth tried to unite civility and truth in a few short sentences.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “elevation”: -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Elizabeth could safely say that it was a great happiness where that was the case, and with equal sincerity could add that she firmly believed and rejoiced in his domestic comforts.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “comfort”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + fort (Latin fortis, "strong"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: You see on what a footing we are.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “footing”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To draw preliminary outline or main features of
vocabulary.context: We seem to have been designed for each other.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “design”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A rite or ceremony performed with religious reverence
vocabulary.context: Collins was gratified; and with a more smiling solemnity replied—
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “solemnity”: sol (Latin solus, "alone" / sol, "sun") + -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A setting of the mind or thoughts upon a subject
vocabulary.context: Jane looked well, and Elizabeth had little opportunity of studying her spirits, amidst the various engagements which the kindness of her aunt had reserved for them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “study”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Elizabeth could safely say that it was a great happiness where that was the case, and with equal sincerity could add that she firmly believed and rejoiced in his domestic comforts.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “rejoice”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Departing guests received formal speeches of thanks and good wishes.

significance: Collins's speech is comic self-praise disguised as humility.
discussionQuestions: Is Charlotte content or simply resigned?

How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with marriage and money?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXXVIII,” how does Austen show farewells at Hunsford? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XXXVIII, how does Austen develop the idea of farewells at Hunsford? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXVIII develops the idea of farewells at Hunsford. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXXVIII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of farewells at Hunsford. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXXVIII suggests about farewells at Hunsford. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's irony and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses irony in Chapter XXXVIII to complicate the reader's understanding of farewells at Hunsford. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXVIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of farewells at Hunsford responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXXVIII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of farewells at Hunsford follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XXXVIII and its treatment of farewells at Hunsford. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's irony and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XXXVIII as evidence for a larger claim about farewells at Hunsford in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXXVIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of farewells at Hunsford. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Is Charlotte content or simply resigned? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are parcels, poultry, consternation, elevation, comforts. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “At length the chaise arrived, the trunks were fastened on, the parcels placed within, and it was pronounced to be ready.” Webster's says: A portion of anything taken separately. Now the word history: “parcel”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “poultry”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “consternation”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Departing guests received formal speeches of thanks and good wishes. Why does this chapter matter? Collins's speech is comic self-praise disguised as humility. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see irony, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to farewells at Hunsford.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Irony, Characterization, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

She had spent six weeks with great enjoyment; and the pleasure of being with Charlotte, and the kind attentions she had received, must make her feel the obliged. segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Irony, Characterization, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXXVIII,” how does Austen show farewells at Hunsford? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about farewells at Hunsford, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how irony shapes farewells at Hunsford. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
